claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
High oxygen partial pressure causes rapid formation of an external oxide scale.
The oxide scale is brittle and dual-phase.
The oxide scale consists primarily of Al2O3 and Cr-rich oxides.
Rapid oxide-scale formation and thickening produce high internal stresses.
Internal stress accumulation results in poor adhesion between the oxide scale and the underlying alloy.
Poor oxide–alloy interfacial adhesion causes oxide-scale spallation.
Oxide spallation exposes fresh metal to the oxidizing atmosphere.
Exposure of fresh metal after spallation promotes further cracking and degradation of structural integrity.
The spallation-and-cracking sequence can ultimately cause catastrophic failure.
At 800°C, increasing oxygen partial pressure from about 0.1 atm to about 1 atm will produce a thicker oxide scale.
At 800°C, the high-oxygen-pressure condition will produce poorer scale adhesion than the low-oxygen-pressure condition.
At 800°C, the high-oxygen-pressure condition will produce more interfacial cracking and spallation than the low-oxygen-pressure condition.
Lower oxygen partial pressure will slow oxide growth and delay or reduce catastrophic failure relative to the baseline condition.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply near 800°C over oxygen partial pressures of approximately 0.1–1 atm.
The proposed oxidation mechanism may not govern degradation under reducing-gas exposure.
Oxide thickness, phases, adhesion, crack density, spallation, and residual stress can be compared after exposures at 0.1 and 1 atm oxygen partial pressure.
